Name: Oracle Bone Inscriptions
Metaphysical Tags: Apophatic–Aporetic (Unknowable), Becoming (Process Ontology), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Phenomenology (Experiential), Grid (Systematic Structuralism)
Short Description: Oracle Bone Inscriptions are the earliest substantial corpus of Chinese writing, produced mainly during the late Shang dynasty for royal divination. Short inscriptions carved into ox scapulae and turtle plastrons record charges concerning warfare, harvests, weather, illness, childbirth, sacrifice, and royal affairs, often followed by prognostications and sometimes verification of the result. The practice centered on the king and court diviners, who addressed royal ancestors, nature powers, and the high god Di. The bones therefore preserve both ritual procedure and administrative memory, revealing how Shang kingship presented itself as the privileged mediator between the living court and powerful unseen agents.

Name: Bronze Inscriptions
Metaphysical Tags: Becoming (Process Ontology), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Monism (Single Principle), Phenomenology (Experiential)
Short Description: Bronze Inscriptions are texts cast, and sometimes engraved, on ritual bronze vessels from the late Shang through the Zhou periods. They commemorate appointments, military campaigns, land grants, legal settlements, marriages, ancestral dedications, and the circumstances in which vessels were commissioned. Unlike oracle bones, bronze inscriptions were attached to durable lineage objects used in ritual and preserved across generations, but the two media overlapped in religious and political function rather than representing a clean replacement of divination by secular recordkeeping. Collectively, the inscriptions form a dispersed archive of royal and aristocratic memory, authority, and kinship.

Metaphysical Tags: Phenomenology (Experiential), Becoming (Process Ontology), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Dialectics (Conflict), Subversion (Negation)
Short Description: The Book of Songs (Shijing) is an anthology of 305 poems composed and transmitted across several centuries of the Zhou period. The collection includes regional airs, court odes, and sacrificial hymns addressing courtship, labor, war, agriculture, political complaint, dynastic memory, and ancestral ritual. Some poems probably drew on local song traditions, while others were produced for aristocratic, royal, or ceremonial settings; their precise authorship and collection history remain uncertain. Later Confucian interpretation transformed the anthology into a major source of moral, political, literary, and educational authority.

Short Description: The I Ching (Yijing) is a layered classic whose oldest stratum, the Zhouyi, was a Western Zhou divination manual organized around sixty-four hexagrams and their line statements. The core text supplies compressed judgments and images for interpreting uncertain situations rather than a systematic philosophical argument. During the Warring States and early imperial periods, commentarial layers later grouped as the Ten Wings recast the work in ethical, cosmological, and political terms and helped associate it with yin–yang and correlative thought. The resulting classic became simultaneously a divination text, a philosophical resource, and a major object of Confucian scholarship.

Short Description: The Book of Documents (Shujing) is a composite anthology of speeches, proclamations, counsels, and narratives attributed to rulers and ministers from legendary antiquity through the Zhou dynasty. Its chapters were produced and transmitted at different times: some preserve early political and ritual material, while others are later reconstructions written in archaizing styles. Arranged as a history of legitimate rulership, the collection presents virtue, ritual, and Heaven’s mandate as standards by which dynasties rise and fall. Tradition associated Confucius with its transmission, but modern scholarship treats it as a layered corpus shaped by court scribes, teachers, and later editors.

Name: Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Becoming (Process Ontology), Dialectics (Conflict), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Subversion (Negation)
Short Description: The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) is the terse official chronicle of the State of Lu, covering the years 722–481 BCE. Its brief entries record accessions, deaths, diplomatic meetings, wars, rituals, eclipses, and disasters, usually without narrative explanation. Later tradition attributed its editing to Confucius and read its wording, titles, and omissions as a system of encoded moral judgment. That influential doctrine of subtle “praise and blame” belongs chiefly to the commentary traditions and should not be treated as an uncontested feature of the bare annals themselves. The received chronicle was compiled from Lu court records around the fifth century BCE.

Short Description: The Analects (Lunyu) is a layered collection of sayings, conversations, and remembered actions attributed to Confucius. Its material was transmitted and compiled by several generations of disciples and later Confucian communities, and different books of the received text probably reflect different stages of formation. The collection centers on learning, ritual, humane conduct, filial responsibility, exemplary rulership, and the cultivation of the junzi. It gained increasing authority under the Han and later became one of the Four Books in the Song dynasty, when it was established at the center of the classical educational curriculum.

Short Description: The Art of War is a compact Warring States military treatise traditionally attributed to Sun Wu. Its received form probably reflects more than one stage of composition and editing. The text treats warfare as costly and dangerous and argues that victory depends on intelligence, planning, deception, logistics, terrain, timing, and adaptation rather than heroic courage alone. Its ideal commander shapes conditions in advance, attacks plans and alliances, and seeks to win with the least possible expenditure of lives and resources.

Short Description: The Dao De Jing is a compact, layered collection of aphoristic verses centered on the Dao as the elusive source and course of the world. It develops themes of non-coercive action, receptivity, simplicity, reversal, emptiness, and the strength of what appears weak or yielding. Politically, many chapters advise rulers to limit intrusive action and avoid multiplying desires, laws, warfare, and displays of power. Traditionally attributed to Laozi, the received text is better understood as the result of multiple collections and editorial stages within the late Warring States period.

Short Description: Mozi is a large composite corpus produced by Mozi and successive Mohist communities during the Warring States period. Its diverse chapters reflect the work of an organized movement of teachers, debaters, administrators, and technical specialists rather than a single act of authorship.

Metaphysical Tags: Phenomenology (Experiential), Becoming (Process Ontology), Dialectics (Conflict), Monism (Single Principle), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Subversion (Negation)
Short Description: Mencius (Mengzi) is a collection of dialogues, debates, and sayings attributed to Mencius and probably compiled by his disciples or later members of his school. The text argues that human beings possess incipient moral tendencies that can be cultivated and that legitimate government depends on benevolence, economic security, and responsiveness to the people. It presents Mencius confronting rulers over war, taxation, profit, and the moral limits of political authority, including the legitimacy of removing a tyrant. The work was influential under the Han but attained its later canonical centrality as one of the Four Books during the Song dynasty.

Short Description: The Shang Jun Shu (Book of Lord Shang) is a composite Warring States corpus associated with Shang Yang’s reforms and later Qin-oriented statecraft. It advocates clear standards, household registration, mutual responsibility, rewards and punishments, and policies that privilege agriculture and military service. Its chapters differ in date and argument: some attack inherited status and moral persuasion, while others emphasize material incentives, administrative control, and the ruler’s management of officials. The text consistently subordinates private interests to state strength, but its political program is broader than punishment and coercion alone.

Short Description: Zhuangzi is a composite literary–philosophical corpus centered on writings attributed to Zhuang Zhou and expanded by later authors. Through parables, dialogues, jokes, dreams, and radical changes of perspective, it questions fixed distinctions, rigid moral programs, and confidence in language. The text explores spontaneity, transformation, mortality, skill, and forms of freedom that do not depend on public status or political success. Its chapters do not present a single uniform doctrine, but together they became foundational to later understandings of philosophical Daoism.

The manuscripts preserve a distinct Sun Bin military tradition, although the exact stages of authorship and compilation remain uncertain.

Short Description: Xunzi is a collection of essays associated with Xun Kuang and shaped by later editors. It argues that unregulated human dispositions lead to conflict and that ethical conduct must be produced through conscious effort, teachers, ritual, standards, and institutions. Ritual is presented not merely as inherited ceremony but as a deliberate means of channeling desire, distributing resources, and creating stable social distinctions. The work combines moral cultivation with sustained analysis of language, knowledge, law, administration, and political power without simply collapsing Confucianism into Legalism.

Short Description: Han Feizi is a large statecraft corpus primarily associated with Han Fei, although the authorship of some chapters is disputed. It develops a political system based on public standards and laws (fa), administrative techniques for controlling officials (shu), and the positional power of the ruler (shi). The text criticizes reliance on moral persuasion and personal trust, emphasizing measurable performance, rewards, punishments, and protection against ministerial manipulation. It also adapts Daoist language and contains influential commentaries on the Laozi, so it should not be described as simply rejecting Daoist thought.

Manuscripts such as those from Shuihudi reveal detailed procedures governing investigations, labor, property, agriculture, official accountability, military service, and punishment. The corpus is practical administrative documentation, not a single complete Qin legal code.

Short Description: Huainanzi is an encyclopedic philosophical compendium presented to Emperor Wu in 139 BCE and compiled by scholars at the court of Liu An, Prince of Huainan. It synthesizes Daoist, cosmological, medical, military, historical, and political materials rather than representing a single philosophical school. Across its chapters, cosmic processes, self-cultivation, knowledge, and government are treated as interconnected, with effective rule often linked to adaptation and restraint. Its court setting makes it a sophisticated proposal for imperial statecraft, but not simply a state-commissioned Daoist manual.

Its chapters connect interpretations of the Spring and Autumn Annals with Heaven–human correlations, yin–yang thought, ritual, ethics, and political order, but they do not all express a single consistent doctrine. The work is best treated as a layered corpus associated with Dong Zhongshu’s intellectual legacy rather than a unified book written entirely by him.

Short Description: The Book of Rites (Liji) is a collection of Warring States and Han essays on ritual, education, mourning, music, family relations, government, and moral cultivation. Rather than preserving one uniform system, the work gathers competing formulations of li as ceremony, social norm, embodied training, and political order. Its canonization helped make ritual discourse central to later Confucian education and governance.

Short Description: Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) is a universal history extending from legendary antiquity to the early Han dynasty. Sima Qian organized the work into basic annals, chronological tables, institutional treatises, hereditary houses, and biographies, creating a structure capable of presenting rulers, institutions, states, and individuals within one historical field. Its narratives combine archival research, inherited traditions, eyewitness information, and literary construction. The work often gives sustained attention to defeated, disgraced, marginal, or morally ambiguous figures, making history a record of contingency, character, power, and the unstable relationship between virtue and success.

Government officials defend intervention as necessary for revenue, frontier defense, and control of wealthy merchants, while invited scholars criticize profit-seeking government, heavy burdens, and the erosion of agricultural and moral priorities. The received work is not a verbatim transcript but a structured series of arguments. Huan Kuan compiled it in the first century BCE during the reign of Emperor Xuan.

Metaphysical Tags: Becoming (Process Ontology), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Dialectics (Conflict), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Phenomenology (Experiential), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: Huangdi Neijing is a composite medical canon rather than a work authored by the Yellow Emperor. The received corpus centers on the Suwen and Lingshu, largely structured as dialogues between Huangdi and medical advisers. Its diverse layers explain the body through qi, yin–yang, Five Phases, seasonal cycles, organs, channels, emotions, environment, and patterns of imbalance, while discussing prevention, diagnosis, acupuncture, and regimen. The text favors naturalistic and correlative explanations of illness, but its materials developed over time and do not always form a single internally consistent system.

Name: Book of Han (Hanshu)
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Monism (Single Principle), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Becoming (Process Ontology), Dialectics (Conflict)
Arts and Sciences Tags: History, Political Science/Law, Astronomy, Economics, Education, Philosophy
Short Description: Book of Han (Hanshu) is the official dynastic history of the Western Han, completed in 111 CE. Modeled on the Shiji but organized around a single dynasty, it combines imperial annals, chronological tables, treatises on institutions and knowledge, and biographies into a comprehensive account of the Former Han and Wang Mang’s interregnum. The project was begun by Ban Biao, substantially composed by Ban Gu, and completed after Ban Gu’s death through major contributions by Ban Zhao, with assistance on specialized sections. Drawing heavily on court archives, the Hanshu established the model for later official dynastic histories.

Name: Prajnaparamita Sutras (Bōrě Bōluómìduō Jīng)
Metaphysical Tags: Apophatic–Aporetic (Unknowable), Subversion (Negation), Dialectics (Conflict), Monism (Single Principle), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Becoming (Process Ontology), Phenomenology (Experiential)
Short Description: The Prajnaparamita Sutras are a large family of Mahayana scriptures composed in India over several centuries and translated into Chinese beginning in the late second century CE. Their central themes include the perfection of wisdom, emptiness, non-attainment, the bodhisattva path, and the critique of treating concepts or practices as possessing fixed essence. The Chinese corpus contains texts of different lengths and dates and is therefore neither a single book nor an originally Chinese composition. Translation, commentary, recitation, copying, and ritual use made the tradition foundational for Sanlun, Tiantai, Chan, and wider East Asian Buddhism. Major Chinese translations were produced by teams associated with Lokakṣema, Dharmarakṣa, Kumārajīva, and Xuanzang.

Name: Lotus Sutra (early Chinese translations, Fǎhuá Jīng)
Metaphysical Tags: Apophatic–Aporetic (Unknowable), Phenomenology (Experiential), Becoming (Process Ontology), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Dialectics (Conflict), Monism (Single Principle), Subversion (Negation)
Short Description: The Lotus Sutra is an Indian Mahayana scripture known in China through several translations. It presents earlier teachings as skillful means and proclaims the One Vehicle, the broad possibility of Buddhahood, and the continuing salvific activity of the Buddha. Its Chinese versions strongly emphasize the merit of hearing, teaching, copying, reciting, and preserving the scripture. The text became central to East Asian exegetical, devotional, and ritual traditions, especially Tiantai, but it did not replace ritual or lineage with scripture alone. The major early Chinese versions were produced by Dharmarakṣa in 286 CE and by Kumārajīva and his translation team in 406 CE.

Name: Vimalakirti Sutra (Wéimójié Jīng)
Metaphysical Tags: Apophatic–Aporetic (Unknowable), Phenomenology (Experiential), Subversion (Negation), Dialectics (Conflict), Monism (Single Principle), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Becoming (Process Ontology)
Short Description: The Vimalakirti Sutra is an Indian Mahayana scripture translated repeatedly into Chinese. Centered on the lay bodhisattva Vimalakirti, it uses dialogue, paradox, humor, miraculous scenes, and the celebrated silence on nonduality to explore emptiness, skillful means, and compassionate activity within the world. Monks and advanced bodhisattvas are repeatedly challenged, but the text does not simply reject monasticism or scholarship; it destabilizes fixed claims to spiritual superiority. In China, its popularity among monastics and literati helped articulate an influential ideal of the spiritually accomplished lay practitioner. The principal extant Chinese versions are attributed to Zhi Qian, Kumārajīva, and Xuanzang.
